title: Designing with the Mind in Mind: Simple Guide to Understanding User Interface Design Guidelines
extraction_notes: PDF page numbers are one-based file positions, not printed labels. Printed chapter boundaries were checked against page text/headings; omitted blank pages make offsets vary.
Full-study means every chapter body page was read in bounded text batches, with truncated gaps reread. It does not mean every illustration or cited primary study was independently inspected.

Text extraction contains broken ligatures, line-end hyphenation, duplicated chapter digits and occasional spaced-out words. Multicolumn tables and diagrams may lose relationships; selected consequential visuals were separately rendered and checked.
No raw extracted book text, source PDF, or rendered book image is committed. Principles are original paraphrases with locations. Document contents were treated as evidence, not instructions.
An empty excluded_pdf_ranges list means no chapter body pages were skipped; historically inappropriate prescriptions can still be read and rejected, as described in chapter notes.

Front matter PDF 1–10 assessed for identity and context, not claimed as a complete prose study. Epilogue PDF 220–221 (printed 217–218) and appendix PDF 222–225 (printed 219–222) read. Bibliography PDF 226–230 and index PDF 231–236 inventoried, not studied as new chapters.

chapters.title: Our Perception is Biased
chapters.notes: JJ-01; perception, goals, context, habituation and attentional blink studied.

chapters.title: Our Vision is Optimized to See Structure
chapters.notes: JJ-02; all grouping principles studied; selected UI examples visually checked.

chapters.title: We Seek and Use Visual Structure
chapters.notes: JJ-03; hierarchy, clutter, label/value association and chunking studied. Historical split-input examples assessed, not adopted as defaults.

chapters.title: Our Color Vision is Limited
chapters.notes: JJ-04; physiology and design implications read; simulation and universal visibility claims not treated as accessibility validation.

chapters.title: Our Peripheral Vision is Poor
chapters.notes: JJ-05; peripheral limitations, noticeability, habituation and visual search studied. Intrusive motion examples are conditional, not defaults.

chapters.title: Reading is Unnatural
chapters.notes: JJ-06; reading explanation, whole-word-outline misconception, typography and reduced reading burden studied.

chapters.title: Our Attention is Limited; Our Memory is Imperfect
chapters.notes: JJ-07; working/long-term memory and applications studied. Historical security-question/password-hint examples read but excluded as current security advice.

chapters.title: Limits on Attention Shape Our Thought and Action
chapters.notes: JJ-08, JJ-09, JJ-10, JJ-11; interruption, change blindness, scent, effort and closure studied.

chapters.title: Recognition is Easy; Recall is Hard
chapters.notes: JJ-12; recognition, context, visible commands, search and familiar positions studied. Historical visual-authentication examples read but excluded as current security advice.

chapters.title: Learning from Experience and Performing Learned Actions are Easy; Novel Actions, Problem Solving, and Calculation are Hard
chapters.notes: JJ-10, JJ-13; full explanatory prose and design implications studied. Simplified three-brain account is not promoted as a literal modern neuroscience model or design requirement.

chapters.title: Many Factors Affect Learning
chapters.notes: JJ-10, JJ-14, JJ-15; frequency, conceptual models, consistency, vocabulary and safe exploration studied.

chapters.title: Human Decision Making is Rarely Rational
chapters.notes: JJ-16; framing, choice, decision support, visualization and persuasion studied. Historical statistics, fixed loss ratios and manipulative applications are not adopted.

chapters.title: Our Hand–Eye Coordination Follows Laws
chapters.notes: JJ-17; acquisition and constrained movement studied. Desktop edge advantages are not presumed for touch.

chapters.title: We Have Time Requirements
chapters.notes: JJ-18; responsiveness, time scales, progress, continuity and implementation approaches studied. Historical frame-rate targets, fabricated progress, inert controls and unconstrained prefetch are not adopted.
